blocks.text: Quick verdict

Decodo is one of the most natural NetNut replacements: its 115M+ residential pool and near-perfect benchmark success rates match or exceed what NetNut offered, it sells ISP proxies for former static-residential users, and its published pricing ($35 for 10 GB, $275 for 100 GB) is easy to budget. City, ZIP and ASN targeting, SOCKS5 and scraping APIs cover most former NetNut use cases, and the free trial lets you test before moving production traffic.

Decodo vs NetNut used to be a close mid-market comparison. Since the FBI seized NetNut's domains in July 2026, after Google linked its residential network to the Popa botnet, the question has become how to move from NetNut to a provider like Decodo. This page explains what happened, compares Decodo with NetNut's former offer, and lays out a safe migration plan for scraping and account workloads.
What happened to NetNut?

NetNut stopped being a normal buying option on July 2, 2026. That day the FBI and IRS Criminal Investigation seized NetNut-related domains, and Google published research linking the network's residential exit nodes to the Popa botnet, which it estimated at two million or more hijacked home devices. NetNut's parent, Alarum Technologies, rejects the allegations, but its main domains went on to show seizure banners and its share price fell sharply. Whatever the final legal outcome, routing business traffic through that infrastructure now carries legal and reputational risk.

blocks.text: Decodo in 2026: what you get

Decodo is the 2024 rebrand of Smartproxy, one of the most popular mid-market providers. Its residential network is advertised at 115 million IPs across 195+ locations, and independent benchmarks put its success rate around 99.9% with sub-second response times. Every plan includes the full pool plus city, state, ZIP and ASN targeting, and the dashboard is one of the easiest to set up. Decodo also sells datacenter, ISP and mobile proxies and a family of scraping APIs.

Decodo (formerly Smartproxy) sits between the budget brands and the enterprise giants. It gives every customer the full 115M+ residential pool, city and ZIP targeting, and a self-service dashboard that most people can configure in minutes. Proxyway's annual tests ranked its pool second only to Oxylabs in size among the providers it tested, at a price well below enterprise level, which is why Decodo shows up on almost every shortlist.

Strengths: Large 115M+ pool at a mid-market price; Near-perfect success rates in independent tests; Clean, fast self-service onboarding; Scraping APIs available when raw proxies are not enough. Weak spots: Plan traffic does not roll over; Published pricing stops at 100 GB; beyond that you need a quote; More expensive per GB than budget brands.
What NetNut offered, and how Decodo compares

Before the seizure, NetNut was best known for ISP-sourced static residential proxies and a fast rotating residential network aimed at scraping, ad verification and brand-protection teams. Its residential rates generally ran from about $1.87 to $3.53 per GB on larger plans, with higher effective prices on entry plans. Decodo covers much of the same ground: datacenter, isp, mobile, scraping apis (web, serp, e-commerce, social) sit alongside its residential network, which advertises 115M+ IPs in 195+ countries.
What former NetNut customers need, and whether Decodo
delivers

Most NetNut accounts were built around three things: static ISP IPs for long-lived sessions, rotating residential traffic with US state and city targeting, and high concurrency for scraping. On static ISP-style IPs, Decodo's answer is yes; its other products are datacenter, ISP, mobile, scraping APIs (web, SERP, e-commerce, social). On rotating residential targeting, Decodo offers country, state, city, ZIP and ASN in 195+ countries, with rotating or sticky sessions with configurable duration. On billing, Decodo uses pay-as-you-go or monthly plans; top-ups at the same per-GB rate, and unused traffic is handled as follows: plan traffic resets monthly; PAYG for bursty work. Map each of your old NetNut zones to one of these before you migrate, so nothing breaks on the day you switch.
Decodo pricing

Decodo sells residential traffic at $4/GB pay-as-you-go with no commitment, or on monthly plans: 3 GB for $11.25 ($3.75/GB), 10 GB for $35, 25 GB at $3.25/GB, 50 GB for $150 and 100 GB for $275 ($2.75/GB). Top-ups are billed at your plan's rate, so you are not pushed into the next tier.

Quick cost check for Decodo: 10 GB comes to $35 (10 GB plan, $3.50/GB), and 100 GB comes to $275 (100 GB plan, $2.75/GB). NetNut's larger plans used to run about $1.87-$3.53/GB, so compare against what you actually paid rather than NetNut's headline rate.
How to migrate from NetNut to Decodo
1. Export your NetNut usage history and list the countries, cities and session types you actually used, so you can map them to Decodo's targeting (country, state, city, ZIP and ASN).
2. Test before you commit. Decodo's testing option: free trial (about 100 MB) on residential. Run your real targets for a day on the smallest purchase before moving production traffic.
3. Swap the gateway host and credentials in your scraper or browser profiles. Decodo supports HTTP, HTTPS, SOCKS5.
4. Compare success rate, response time and cost per successful request against your old NetNut baseline, then move traffic over in stages.
5. Remove any NetNut SDKs, browser extensions or endpoints from your systems, and rotate any credentials that were stored alongside them.
Where Decodo fits best
General web scraping: strong fit. Why: a large pool and near-perfect benchmark success rates.
SERP and rank tracking: strong fit. Why: a dedicated SERP scraping API plus city targeting.
Social media and multi-account management: strong fit. Why: sticky sessions, sub-users and an easy dashboard.
E-commerce price and stock monitoring: strong fit. Why: ZIP targeting and a ready-made e-commerce API.
Ad verification and geo-testing: strong fit. Why: wide coverage with city and ASN targeting.
Tight budgets: workable. Why: it is mid-priced, not cheap.
Protocols and sessions

Decodo supports HTTP, HTTPS, SOCKS5 and offers rotating or sticky sessions with configurable duration. Targeting covers country, state, city, ZIP and ASN across 195+ countries. Like NetNut's residential gateway, it works through a single backconnect endpoint with location and session options passed in the username, plus IP whitelisting.
How to vet a residential proxy provider after NetNut

NetNut's customers did not choose to route traffic through a botnet; they bought what looked like a standard enterprise service. The lesson is to check sourcing before you buy, not after. Whichever provider replaces NetNut for you, Decodo included, run through these checks:
How are residential IPs sourced? Look for an opt-in SDK or app programme with clear user
consent and compensation, and ask which partner apps are involved.
Does the provider publish an ethics or sourcing policy, and has it been audited or certified (for
example AppEsteem or ISO 27001)?
What KYC does the provider apply to customers, and which target categories are restricted?
Strict onboarding is a good sign, not an inconvenience.
How does it handle abuse reports, and is there a named legal entity and jurisdiction behind the
service?
Can you get contractual assurances, such as a data-processing agreement, if your compliance
team needs them?
Bottom line

NetNut is no longer a provider you can plan around, so the real decision is which network replaces it. Decodo is strongest for small and mid-size scraping teams and developers who want enterprise-like quality without contracts, starts at $4/GB pay-as-you-go; plans from $3.75/GB (3 GB for $11.25), and offers free trial (about 100 MB) on residential. Test it on your own targets for a day, compare cost per successful request with your old NetNut baseline, and move production traffic in stages.
